issue: Self-introduction at a small meetup is casual/conversational, not keynote-level speaking; no narrative arc, opening impact, or audience-centered hook needed
original_question: Introduce yourself at a small meetup.
suggested_rewrite: Give a 60-second opening to a small audience of 10–15 people to kick off a community event — introduce the event theme and why everyone is here.
new_tips: Open with the shared purpose that brought people to the room
Set an energetic, welcoming tone that gets people excited for what's next
End with a clear handoff: what happens first and why it matters

issue: Sharing a fun fact with a group is casual chitchat, not keynote practice; no presentation structure or narrative is required
original_question: Share a fun fact about a topic you know well.
suggested_rewrite: Open a short talk to a small audience by delivering one surprising fact about a topic you know well, then briefly explain why it matters.
new_tips: Lead with the surprising hook before revealing the topic
Explain the fact's significance in one or two clear sentences
Invite the audience to think about what it means for them

issue: Describing a vacation to a group is casual storytelling, not keynote speaking; tips reinforce casual register rather than any structured talk format
original_question: Describe your favorite vacation to a group.
suggested_rewrite: Give a brief talk to a small group about a place you've visited — use it to share one insight about the world or yourself that the trip revealed.
new_tips: Open with a vivid single image that transports the audience
Build toward one clear insight or lesson, not just a highlight reel
Close with a line that makes the audience want to see it for themselves

issue: Sharing a New Year's resolution with a group is casual sharing, not keynote practice; no structure, narrative arc, or audience-centered purpose
original_question: Share your New Year's resolution with a group.
suggested_rewrite: Give a brief 60-second talk encouraging a group to set a goal for the new year — share your own resolution as an example and make the case for why it matters.
new_tips: Open with why goal-setting is worth the group's attention, not just your goal
Use your personal resolution to illustrate a broader point
Close with a call to action: encourage the audience to commit to something

issue: Sharing your weekend highlight with the team is water-cooler conversation, not keynote practice; contradicts the mode's focus on narrative arc and opening impact
original_question: Share your weekend highlight with the team.
suggested_rewrite: Open a Monday team meeting with a 60-second energizer: share one moment from your weekend that connects to a value or goal the team cares about.
new_tips: Pick a moment that has a relatable point, not just entertainment value
Keep the story tight — one scene, one insight
Connect back to the team or the week ahead to justify the air time

issue: No context for what department, what results, or what time period; vague enough that a user won't know where to begin
original_question: Present quarterly results to your department.
suggested_rewrite: Present a mixed-result quarter to your department: one key metric improved, one declined. Explain what happened and what you'll do differently next quarter.
new_tips: Lead with the headline — one number or outcome that frames everything else
Own the miss: explain what drove the decline with specifics, not excuses
Close with a concrete plan for next quarter, not vague optimism

issue: Emceeing a holiday party is event hosting, not a keynote speech; tips are vague platitudes ('energy high with humor and warmth') and don't coach any speechmaking skill
original_question: Emcee a company holiday party.
suggested_rewrite: Open a company holiday celebration with a 90-second address: acknowledge the year's highs and lows honestly, celebrate the team, and set a festive tone for the evening.
new_tips: Open with one specific moment or win from the year that the whole room can feel proud of
Keep the tone warm but not saccharine — authenticity beats cheerfulness
End with a toast line that gives everyone a shared, memorable moment

issue: A safety briefing is a compliance task, not keynote speaking; even the difficultyNote frames it as 'mandatory topic' which signals it doesn't belong in a keynote practice mode
original_question: Deliver a safety briefing in an engaging way.
suggested_rewrite: Give a short talk to a team explaining why a specific safety protocol matters — make the case using a real scenario so people actually remember and follow it.
new_tips: Open with a real-world consequence story, not a list of rules
Frame compliance as protecting people, not just avoiding liability
Close with one memorable takeaway that sticks after people leave the room

issue: An impromptu speech prompt belongs in the casual/impromptu mode, not keynote; the tips are generic and don't address keynote-specific skills like narrative arc or stage presence
original_question: Give an impromptu speech when asked to speak unexpectedly.
suggested_rewrite: You've just been called to the stage unexpectedly at an industry event. Give a 90-second off-the-cuff keynote-style response to the event's central theme.
new_tips: Take one beat to identify the single most relevant thing you can say to this room
Open with a concrete claim or observation, not 'I wasn't expecting this'
Close with something the audience can take away — make the moment count

issue: No topic or domain is specified; 'a dry topic' is so open-ended it provides no useful constraint to practice against
original_question: Give an informative talk that makes a dry topic fascinating.
suggested_rewrite: Give a talk that makes supply chain logistics — or another notoriously dry business topic you know — genuinely compelling to a general audience.
new_tips: Open with a surprising consequence of this topic that affects everyday life
Use one vivid analogy to make the mechanism click for a non-expert
Close with a 'so what' that makes the audience glad they paid attention

issue: Near-duplicate of keynote_5-6_006 ('Present a TEDx-style talk on a personal passion'); both ask for a TED-style narrative speech with personal hook and universal lesson
original_question: Give a TED talk that introduces a new concept.
suggested_rewrite: Give a TED-style talk that introduces a concept your field takes for granted but the general public has never heard of — make it feel urgent and exciting.
new_tips: Name the concept early and give it a memorable framing the audience can hold onto
Build through progressive revelation: let understanding unfold rather than front-loading
Close with a specific implication that makes the audience see something in their life differently

issue: No topic is given; 'present to the UN or equivalent' is an intimidating context without any subject anchor — the user has no idea what they're supposed to be arguing for
original_question: Present to the United Nations or equivalent body.
suggested_rewrite: Present a 2-minute address to an international body (like the UN) making the case for urgent global cooperation on one specific issue — climate, pandemic preparedness, or tech governance.
new_tips: Open by naming the shared stake — what all nations lose if this issue goes unaddressed
Present your proposal in plain language that survives translation
Close with a concrete ask: a resolution, a commitment, a next meeting

issue: 'Integrate live demonstration' assumes a physical prop or screen — it's unclear what the user is supposed to demo in a speech-recording app context, making the tip about 'backup plans for technical failures' nonsensical
original_question: Give a keynote that integrates live demonstration.
suggested_rewrite: Give a keynote that weaves a simulated live demonstration into your narrative — describe what you'd show on screen or stage, and use the reveal moment as the emotional peak of the talk.
new_tips: Narrate the demo as if the audience is watching it unfold in real time
Make the demo illustrate your core claim, not just show a feature
Use the moment of revelation to anchor your key message

issue: 'A speech that will be quoted for decades' is aspirational framing, not a scenario — it gives the user no context, audience, or topic to work from; it's pure outcome without any setup
original_question: Give a speech that will be quoted for decades.
suggested_rewrite: Craft and deliver a short but historically significant speech — choose your moment (a movement, a milestone, a crisis) and make it feel like it will outlast the room.
new_tips: Find the one sentence you want people to repeat — build everything toward it
Earn the emotional crescendo: let the argument build before you deliver the defining line
Speak as though history is listening — precision of language matters at this level

issue: Giving a speech in a second language is a linguistic challenge, not a keynote skill; it tests language fluency rather than narrative arc, opening impact, or persuasive structure — and most users won't have a relevant second language
original_question: Give a speech in a second language to a foreign audience.
suggested_rewrite: Give a keynote to an international audience where many attendees are non-native English speakers — adapt your delivery, vocabulary, and cultural references to be universally clear and respectful.
new_tips: Slow your pace deliberately and use concrete rather than idiomatic language
Avoid cultural references that don't travel — replace them with universal human experiences
Make your structure crystal-clear so the argument doesn't depend on every word landing

issue: Near-duplicate of keynote_5-6_011 ('Give an impromptu speech when asked to speak unexpectedly'); both are impromptu speech prompts with nearly identical tips about speaking without preparation
original_question: Give a spontaneous speech at a historic moment.
suggested_rewrite: You're a leader at the exact moment a long-awaited breakthrough is announced — a peace deal, a scientific discovery, an election result. Speak to the room without prepared notes.
new_tips: Read the emotional temperature of the room before your first word
Name what this moment means — don't just describe it, interpret it
Give the audience their role in what comes next: the moment isn't over when you stop speaking

issue: Too generic and unanchored — 'describe your morning routine' has no angle, tension, or reason to practice it; likely to produce flat, list-like responses with no persuasive or explanatory challenge
original_question: Describe your morning routine.
suggested_rewrite: Explain your morning routine to someone who struggles to start their day — and make the case for why one specific habit in it actually makes a difference.
new_tips: Anchor the routine with a concrete detail that makes it feel real and specific
Build toward one insight: what habit matters most and why
Speak as if you're trying to convince them to try it, not just describing your day

issue: Describing the view from your window right now is hyper-situational and luck-dependent; many users are in featureless rooms or will have nothing interesting to describe, making the prompt a dead end
original_question: Describe the view from your window right now.
suggested_rewrite: Describe a place you know well — a street corner, park, or room — as if you're painting it in words for someone who will never see it.
new_tips: Start with the big picture, then zoom into one specific detail that captures the place's character
Use sensory language beyond sight: sound, smell, temperature
End with the feeling the place gives you — not just what it looks like

issue: Asking users to explain a conspiracy theory 'and why people believe it' is ambiguous about stance — it could read as endorsing or legitimizing fringe theories, and the tip 'distinguish belief from evidence' is vague about what the user should conclude
original_question: Explain a conspiracy theory and why people believe it.
suggested_rewrite: Pick a well-known conspiracy theory and explain — without endorsing it — why it spreads and what psychological needs it fulfills for believers.
new_tips: Present the theory factually and neutrally before analyzing it
Name the psychological mechanism at work: mistrust, pattern-seeking, community identity
Distinguish between the appeal of the narrative and the absence of evidence — clearly

issue: No item is specified; 'a common household item' is so open it gives users nothing to anchor on and risks producing generic, aimless responses
original_question: Explain how a common household item works.
suggested_rewrite: Explain how a microwave oven — or another everyday appliance you choose — actually works, at a level that's accurate but accessible to someone with no science background.
new_tips: Start with what the person already observes ('you put food in, it gets hot') before explaining the mechanism
Use one strong analogy to make the underlying science click
End with one surprising fact about the item that reframes how they'll use it

issue: Asking to 'debate both sides of universal basic income' and then share which side you lean toward conflates debate and deliberation; it's also an awkward structure for a solo speech practice session — users need a clearer task frame
original_question: Debate both sides of universal basic income.
suggested_rewrite: Make the strongest possible case for universal basic income to a skeptical audience — address the most common objections and end with a clear position.
new_tips: Open by defining what UBI actually means — many objections rest on a misunderstanding of the proposal
Acknowledge the strongest counterargument before dismantling it with evidence
Close with one concrete, real-world example of a UBI pilot and what it showed

issue: Teaching using only questions is a pedagogical technique, not a casual conversational skill; it requires a back-and-forth listener that doesn't exist in a solo recording session — the user cannot actually use questions interactively
original_question: Teach a complex topic using only questions.
suggested_rewrite: Explain a complex topic by walking your listener through your own thinking process — show how you'd figure it out step by step, not just announce conclusions.
new_tips: Start by framing what makes this topic hard before you start explaining it
Think aloud: let the listener follow the reasoning, not just the outcome
Check in periodically with a rhetorical question to keep the listener oriented

issue: Near-duplicate of casual_5-6_001 ('Explain the trolley problem and argue your position'); this prompt adds 'variants' but covers the same ground with the same ethical reasoning exercise
original_question: Explain the trolley problem variants and their implications.
suggested_rewrite: Walk through the fat man variant of the trolley problem and explain what it reveals about the gap between utilitarian logic and human moral intuition — and what that gap tells us about ethics.
new_tips: Present the specific variant clearly before diving into analysis — don't assume familiarity
Show how the variants isolate different moral variables: agency, proximity, intention
Connect the insight to a real-world ethical decision, not just abstract philosophy

issue: 'Explain the meaning of life using only first principles' is two prompts collapsed into one; first-principles reasoning and the meaning of life are both massive standalone topics — the constraint 'only first principles' is also unexplained
original_question: Explain the meaning of life using only first principles.
suggested_rewrite: Starting from only the basic facts of existence — that we are alive, aware, and temporary — build a logical case for what makes a life meaningful.
new_tips: Define your starting assumptions explicitly before reasoning from them
Build the argument step by step: each claim should follow from the last
End with a framework the listener can apply, not a grand pronouncement

issue: 'Improvised 2-minute speech on a random topic' gives no topic — it's an instruction, not a prompt; the user has nothing concrete to speak about, and the app can't randomly assign a topic in a static JSON prompt
original_question: Deliver an improvised 2-minute speech on a random topic with depth and clarity.
suggested_rewrite: You have 10 seconds to prepare. Your topic: the hidden cost of convenience. Go — deliver a 2-minute speech with a clear thesis and at least two supporting arguments.
new_tips: Commit to a thesis in your first sentence — don't warm up, open strong
Use the thesis-evidence-counterpoint-conclusion structure to give instant shape to the talk
Trust your instincts: at this level, the quality of your thinking under pressure is the point
